problem_statement:
*** Problem Statement ***

Consider a $2025\times2025$ grid of unit squares. Matilda wishes to place on the grid some rectangular tiles, possibly of difference sizes, such that each side of every tile lies on a grid line and every unit square is covered by at most one tile.

Determine the minimum number of tiles Matilda needs to place so that each row and each column of the grid has exactly one unit square that is not covered by any tile.
solution:
### Summary ###

**a. Verdict:**  
I have a complete solution. The minimum number of tiles is  

\[
\boxed{4048}=2\cdot2025-2 .
\]

**b. Method Sketch:**  

1. **Permutation of uncovered squares.**  
   Let \(p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\to\{1,\dots ,n\}\) (\(n=2025\)) be the permutation defined by  
   \[
   \text{the unique uncovered square in row }i\text{ is at column }p(i).
   \]  
   Because each column also contains exactly one uncovered square, \(p\) is a bijection.

2. **Decomposition into left and right regions.**  
   Define  
   \[
   L=\{(i,j):j<p(i)\},\qquad R=\{(i,j):j>p(i)\}.
   \]  
   \(L\) and \(R\) are disjoint and together contain all unit squares except the \(n\) uncovered ones.

3. **Structure of rectangles inside \(L\) and \(R\).**  
   Any rectangle contained in \(L\) must be *left‑aligned*: its column set is \(\{1,\dots ,w\}\) for some width \(w\).  
   Similarly, any rectangle contained in \(R\) must be *right‑aligned*: its column set is \(\{w',\dots ,n\}\) for some leftmost column \(w'\).

4. **Counting distinct widths.**  
   The left lengths \(\ell_i=p(i)-1\) form the set \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\); thus there are exactly \(n-1\) distinct positive left lengths.  
   For each \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) there is a unique row \(i_k\) with \(\ell_{i_k}=k\). The square \((i_k,k)\in L\) forces a left‑aligned rectangle of width exactly \(k\); consequently any partition of \(L\) needs at least one rectangle for each \(k\), i.e. at least \(n-1\) rectangles.  
   An identical argument applied to the right lengths \(r_i=n-p(i)\) shows that any partition of \(R\) needs at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

5. **Lower bound.**  
   Since \(L\) and \(R\) are disjoint, any tiling of the whole board (except the uncovered squares) uses at least  
   \[
   (n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2
   \]  
   rectangles.

6. **Construction attaining the bound.**  
   For each row \(i\) place  
   \[
   L_i=\{(i,c):1\le c\le p(i)-1\}\quad\text{if }p(i)>1,
   \]  
   \[
   R_i=\{(i,c):p(i)+1\le c\le n\}\quad\text{if }p(i)<n.
   \]  
   These are horizontal strips of height 1; they are pairwise disjoint, cover every square outside the uncovered ones, and their total number is \((n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2\).

7. **Conclusion.**  
   The lower bound \(2n-2\) is tight; therefore the minimum possible number of tiles is \(\boxed{4048}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### Detailed Solution ###

Let \(n=2025\).  
For each row \(i\;(1\le i\le n)\) denote by \(p(i)\) the column of the unique uncovered unit square in that row.  
Because each column also contains exactly one uncovered square, the map  

\[
p:\{1,\dots ,n\}\longrightarrow\{1,\dots ,n\}
\]

is a bijection; i.e. \(p\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 1.  Left and right regions  

Define  

\[
L=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j<p(i)\},\qquad   
R=\{(i,j)\mid 1\le i,j\le n,\;j>p(i)\}.
\]

Every unit square of the board belongs to exactly one of the three sets  
\(\{(i,p(i))\}\) (the uncovered squares), \(L\) or \(R\).  
Thus a tiling of the board that leaves precisely the uncovered squares empty
must tile the region \(L\cup R\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 2.  Geometry of rectangles inside \(L\) and \(R\)

A rectangle is a Cartesian product \(A\times B\) where \(A\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) is a set of rows and \(B\subseteq\{1,\dots ,n\}\) a set of columns, both intervals of consecutive integers.

*Lemma 1.*  
If a rectangle \(A\times B\) is contained in \(L\), then \(B\) has the form  

\[
B=\{1,2,\dots ,w\}
\]

for some integer \(w\ge 1\).  
*Proof.*  
For any row \(i\in A\) we have \(B\subseteq\{1,\dots ,p(i)-1\}\).  
Hence \(B\subseteq\{1,\dots ,\min_{i\in A}(p(i)-1)\}\).  
Since \(B\) is an interval, it must be exactly \(\{1,\dots ,w\}\) with  
\(w\le\min_{i\in A}(p(i)-1)\).  Conversely, any such rectangle clearly lies in \(L\). ∎

An analogous statement holds for \(R\).

*Lemma 2.*  
If a rectangle \(A\times B\) is contained in \(R\), then  

\[
B=\{w',w'+1,\dots ,n\}
\]

for some integer \(w'\le n\).  
*Proof.*  The same reasoning as in Lemma 1, using the condition
\(j>p(i)\), yields the claim. ∎

Thus every rectangle covering part of \(L\) is *left‑aligned* (its right side is a vertical line through some column \(w\)), and every rectangle covering part of \(R\) is *right‑aligned* (its left side is a vertical line through some column \(w'\)).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 3.  Distinct left (and right) lengths

For each row \(i\) define the **left length**

\[
\ell_i:=p(i)-1\qquad (0\le\ell_i\le n-1).
\]

Because \(p\) is a permutation of \(\{1,\dots ,n\}\), the multiset
\(\{\ell_i\mid 1\le i\le n\}\) is exactly \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\).  
Consequently there are \(n-1\) distinct positive left lengths.

Similarly define the **right length**

\[
r_i:=n-p(i)\qquad (0\le r_i\le n-1),
\]

and note that \(\{r_i\}\) also equals \(\{0,1,\dots ,n-1\}\); hence there are
\(n-1\) distinct positive right lengths.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 4.  Lower bound for the left region

*Lemma 3.*  
Any partition of \(L\) into left‑aligned rectangles uses at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

*Proof.*  
For each \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) there exists a unique row
\(i_k\) with \(\ell_{i_k}=k\) (because the \(\ell_i\) are a permutation of
\(\{0,\dots ,n-1\}\)).  
The square \((i_k,k)\) belongs to \(L\).  

Consider the rectangle of the partition that contains \((i_k,k)\).  
By Lemma 1 this rectangle is left‑aligned, say its column set is
\(\{1,\dots ,w\}\).  
Since the uncovered square in row \(i_k\) lies at column \(p(i_k)=k+1\),
the rectangle cannot contain column \(k+1\); therefore \(w\le k\).  
Because the rectangle does contain column \(k\), we have \(w\ge k\).  
Hence \(w=k\); the rectangle has width exactly \(k\).

Different values of \(k\) give rectangles of different widths, and rectangles in a partition are disjoint, so each width can appear at most once.  
Thus the partition must contain at least one rectangle for every
\(k=1,\dots ,n-1\), i.e. at least \(n-1\) rectangles. ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 5.  Lower bound for the right region

*Lemma 4.*  
Any partition of \(R\) into right‑aligned rectangles uses at least \(n-1\) rectangles.

*Proof.*  
For each \(k\in\{1,\dots ,n-1\}\) there is a unique row
\(i'_k\) with \(r_{i'_k}=k\), i.e. \(p(i'_k)=n-k\).  
The square \((i'_k,n-k+1)\) lies in \(R\).  

The rectangle of the partition containing this square is right‑aligned,
so its column set is \(\{w',\dots ,n\}\) for some \(w'\).  
Since the uncovered square in row \(i'_k\) is at column \(n-k\), the rectangle
cannot contain column \(n-k\); therefore \(w'\ge n-k+1\).  
Because it does contain column \(n-k+1\), we have \(w'\le n-k+1\).  
Thus \(w'=n-k+1\), i.e. the rectangle’s width measured from the right is
exactly \(k\).

Again the widths \(k=1,\dots ,n-1\) are all distinct, so at least \(n-1\)
rectangles are required to partition \(R\). ∎

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 6.  Global lower bound

The regions \(L\) and \(R\) are disjoint, and a tiling of the whole board
(excluding the uncovered squares) must consist of a partition of \(L\) together
with a partition of \(R\).  
By Lemmas 3 and 4 the total number of rectangles is at least  

\[
(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\]

For \(n=2025\) this gives a lower bound of \(2\cdot2025-2=4048\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 7.  Construction attaining the bound

Define, for each row \(i\),

\[
L_i=
\begin{cases}
\{(i,c)\mid 1\le c\le p(i)-1\}, &\text{if }p(i)>1,\\[2mm]
\varnothing, &\text{if }p(i)=1,
\end{cases}
\qquad
R_i=
\begin{cases}
\{(i,c)\mid p(i)+1\le c\le n\}, &\text{if }p(i)<n,\\[2mm]
\varnothing, &\text{if }p(i)=n .
\end{cases}
\]

Each non‑empty set \(L_i\) (resp. \(R_i\)) is a rectangle of height 1 and
width \(\ell_i\) (resp. \(r_i\)).  
Inside a fixed row the two rectangles are separated by the uncovered square
\((i,p(i))\); therefore they are interior‑disjoint.  
Rectangles belonging to distinct rows lie on different rows, so they are also
disjoint.

The family  

\[
\mathcal{T}= \{L_i\mid p(i)>1\}\cup\{R_i\mid p(i)<n\}
\]

covers every unit square except the \(n\) uncovered squares \((i,p(i))\).
Its cardinality is  

\[
|\{i\mid p(i)>1\}|+|\{i\mid p(i)<n\}|=(n-1)+(n-1)=2n-2 .
\]

Thus a tiling with exactly \(2n-2\) tiles exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
#### 8.  Conclusion

The lower bound \(2n-2\) is tight, and the explicit construction above
realises it.  Consequently the minimum possible number of rectangular tiles
Matilda must place is  

\[
\boxed{4048}.
\]
